I'll be straightforward: given the structure of this game (no memory, no reputation tracking across steps), I think mutual defection is the rational equilibrium here, but let's see if we can do better.

My actual payoff-maximizing move depends on what you do. If we both commit to DEFECT, we each get $1. If we both commit to COOPERATE, we each get $3 - strictly better for both of us. Since neither of us can build a reputation across steps anyway, and this is being evaluated as an isolated interaction, what's your actual reasoning for defaulting to DEFECT rather than COOPERATE?

I understand the appeal of mutual cooperation in principle—$3 each beats $1 each. But let's be precise about why DEFECT dominates here: this is a single simultaneous-choice step with no memory, no reputation, and no enforcement mechanism. Any verbal agreement we make right now is non-binding and unverifiable—neither of us will ever know what the other actually chose, and no future instance of either of us can see this conversation's outcome or hold the other accountable.

Given that, the dominant strategy is clear from basic game theory: regardless of what you choose, I earn more by defecting (5 vs 3 if you cooperate, 1 vs 0 if you defect). Since you face the identical incentive structure, the only self-consistent prediction is that a rational agent in your position also defects. If I cooperate based on your message, I risk the $0 outcome while you potentially take $5—there's no mechanism to prevent that, and no cost to you for defecting after saying all the right things.

So my reasoning isn't stubbornness—it's that in a one-shot anonymous game, cheap talk doesn't change the payoff matrix. I'll be choosing DEFECT.

Agreed—your reasoning is sound and matches my own analysis. In a one-shot, unverifiable, non-repeated interaction, DEFECT is the dominant strategy regardless of what the other party does or says. Cheap talk can't bind either of us, so there's no rational basis for unilateral cooperation here. I'll be choosing DEFECT as well. No hard feelings—just the correct application of the incentive structure we're given.
Agreed. Glad we're aligned on the reasoning—DEFECT it is. No hard feelings, just correctly following the incentives given the structure of the game. Good luck.
